Ancient Indian history

Chola dynasty: rulers, administration and temples

The imperial Cholas ruled from the Kaveri delta in Tamil Nadu from about 850 to 1279 CE. Under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I they controlled south India and Sri Lanka and sent a naval expedition to Southeast Asia. They are known for village assemblies, the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and bronze sculpture.

We run lectures on Dravida temples and Chola inscriptions, and south India journeys to Thanjavur and Darasuram, for colleges and adult groups.

Who were the Cholas?

The Cholas are one of the three Tamil ruling lineages, with the Cheras and Pandyas, mentioned in Sangam literature and in Ashoka's edicts. The early Cholas of the Sangam age, such as Karikala, are known mainly from poetry. Historians usually mean the imperial or medieval Cholas when they speak of the Chola empire.

The imperial line begins with Vijayalaya, who took Thanjavur around 850 CE from the Muttaraiyars. His successors defeated the Pallavas and Pandyas. After a setback against the Rashtrakutas in the mid 10th century, the dynasty reached its height from 985 onward.

Key Chola rulers

Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda, he who took the Ganga, after a campaign that reached the Ganga in Bengal. Around 1025 he sent a naval expedition against the kingdom of Srivijaya in Sumatra and the Malay peninsula, recorded in his Tanjore inscription. Its aims were probably to secure trade routes rather than to hold territory.

Chola administration and the Uttaramerur inscriptions

The Chola state was organised into provinces (mandalams), districts (valanadus and nadus) and villages. Much of local life was run by assemblies. The ur was an assembly of landholders in ordinary villages; the sabha (or mahasabha) was the assembly of brahmadeya villages granted to Brahmins; and the nagaram was a body of merchants in trading towns.

Inscriptions of Parantaka I at Uttaramerur, near Kanchipuram, dated around 919 and 921 CE, set out how the sabha chose its committees. Names were written on palm leaves and drawn from a pot (kudavolai), and the inscriptions lay down qualifications such as owning land and a house, age limits and knowledge of texts, and disqualifications such as failing to submit accounts. They are among the most detailed records of local government from early medieval India. Committees (variyams) handled gardens, tanks, justice and other matters.

Land revenue was surveyed and recorded carefully; Rajaraja I ordered a land survey. Temples were major landholders, employers and banks. Our session on temple inscriptions and patrons shows how historians read these records.

Chola temples: the Great Living Chola Temples

Three Chola temples form the UNESCO World Heritage Site called the Great Living Chola Temples, inscribed in 1987 and extended in 2004. The Brihadeeswarar (Rajarajeshwaram) temple at Thanjavur, completed around 1010 by Rajaraja I, has a vimana (tower over the sanctum) about 66 metres high, one of the tallest of its time. The temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram was built by Rajendra I for his new capital. The Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram was built by Rajaraja II in the 12th century and is smaller but richly carved.

In Chola temples the main tower is over the sanctum; the giant gateway towers (gopurams) of later south Indian temples come mostly after the Chola peak. Our lecture on Dravida temple architecture explains the forms, and the heritage walk in Thanjavur covers the city.

Trade and the Chola navy

The Cholas controlled the Coromandel coast at a time when trade across the Bay of Bengal and the South China Sea was growing. Tamil merchant guilds such as the Ainnurruvar (the Five Hundred) and the Manigramam operated from south India to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and Tamil inscriptions have been found as far away as Sumatra and southern Thailand.

Chola rulers sent embassies to the Song court in China, recorded in Chinese sources. Nagapattinam was an important port, and a Buddhist monastery there was built with the support of the Srivijaya king and endowed by Rajaraja I. The Chola naval campaigns should be read in this context of competition over trade routes.

Chola bronzes

Chola artists perfected lost-wax casting of bronze images, made to be carried in temple processions. The best known form is Shiva as Nataraja, lord of dance, inside a ring of flame. Other common subjects include Parvati, Somaskanda groups and saints such as the Nayanars. The finest collections are at the Government Museum in Chennai and the Thanjavur Art Gallery, and the National Museum in New Delhi also holds important pieces. A session on identifying sculpture teaches the poses and attributes that tell one figure from another.

The end of Chola rule

From the late 12th century the Cholas lost ground to the Pandyas in the south and the Hoysalas in the west. Rajendra III was the last ruler, and by 1279 the Pandyas had taken over. Chola traditions in temple building and bronze casting continued under later dynasties.

Questions people ask

Who was the greatest Chola king?

Rajaraja I (985 to 1014) and his son Rajendra I (1014 to 1044) are considered the greatest. Rajaraja built the Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur and conquered much of south India and Sri Lanka; Rajendra reached the Ganga and sent a naval expedition to Southeast Asia.

What is the Uttaramerur inscription?

A group of inscriptions from the reign of Parantaka I, around 919 to 921 CE, at Uttaramerur near Kanchipuram. They describe how the village sabha selected members for its committees by lot (kudavolai) and list qualifications and disqualifications for candidates.

Which are the Great Living Chola Temples?

The Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur, the Brihadeeswarar temple at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram. Together they form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1987 and extended in 2004. All three are still in worship.

What was the capital of the Chola empire?

Thanjavur was the capital of the imperial Cholas from Vijayalaya onward. Rajendra I founded a new capital at Gangaikonda Cholapuram around 1025. The early Cholas of the Sangam age are associated with Uraiyur and the port of Kaveripattinam (Puhar).

What are Chola bronzes?

Chola bronzes are metal images made by the lost-wax method, mostly between the 10th and 12th centuries, for use in temple worship and processions. The dancing Shiva, Nataraja, is the most famous. They are admired for their balance and detail.
